title: Signals and Levers: Building Thriving Engineering Organizations
gist: Elisabeth Hendrickson and Joel Tosi argue engineering organizations are non-linear adaptive systems where AI rollouts amplify existing bottlenecks rather than removing them, and that leaders should diagnose real ('as done') work before pulling policy or cultural levers, since what's right today can be wrong tomorrow.

themes.theme: Systems Thinking as a Management Lens

insights.claim: Organizations and the software delivery process are non-linear adaptive systems: intervening anywhere in the system produces effects elsewhere that cannot be reliably predicted, so reality cannot be tightly controlled through direct cause-and-effect management.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Hendrickson
insights.so_what: Leaders should expect any policy change to produce unintended downstream effects and should build in observation and course-correction rather than assuming a single fix will hold.
insights.quote: You poke the system, the system is going to poke back.
insights.locator: What Is Systems Thinking?

insights.claim: Software delivery is a sociotechnical system made of an interwoven web of people and technology dependencies, including code written by colleagues, company-managed infrastructure, and open-source or vendor software, such that the whole is greater than and behaves differently from the sum of its parts.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Hendrickson
insights.so_what: Removing or changing any single component (a tool, a team, a vendor) creates a genuinely different system with new emergent behavior, not just a smaller version of the old one.
insights.locator: What Is Systems Thinking?

insights.claim: Organizations are systems nested inside systems at every scale, from an individual team up through department, business unit, company, and the wider competitive ecosystem, which is what makes organizational behavior so hard to reason about linearly.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Hendrickson
insights.so_what: A fix that looks complete at the team level can be undone or distorted by dynamics at the department or company level, so leaders need to check for effects at adjacent system layers.
insights.locator: What Is Systems Thinking?

insights.claim: These nested systems are not static; they are constantly adapting simultaneously at every level, with the organization adapting to competitors and regulation while employees simultaneously adapt to new demands, new teammates, and new technology, which is why linear management logic breaks down.
insights.speaker: Joel Tosi
insights.so_what: Because the system keeps moving while you're intervening, a one-time diagnosis is stale almost immediately, making continuous observation more valuable than periodic planning cycles.
insights.locator: Systems Are Constantly Adapting

themes.theme: AI Rollouts as a System-Wide Amplifier

insights.claim: Organizations running AI rollouts and 'AI transformations' often treat them as a linear program, choosing a tool, rolling it out, and expecting to get value, but this repeatedly fails to produce the intended outcome because AI acts on the whole system, not just the targeted input.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Hendrickson
insights.so_what: Treating an AI rollout as a simple tool deployment rather than a systems-level intervention is a predictable reason enterprise AI initiatives underdeliver relative to expectations.
insights.locator: AI Rollouts and the Limits of Linear Thinking

insights.claim: AI functions as an amplifier that increases output in one part of an organization's system faster than the rest of the system can absorb it, which does not so much move the existing bottleneck as expose bottlenecks and constraints that were not previously visible or problematic.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Hendrickson
insights.so_what: Investors and leaders evaluating AI-adoption claims should look for evidence the surrounding process (review, QA, deployment) was upgraded alongside the AI tool, since output gains alone can just relocate the constraint downstream.
insights.locator: AI Rollouts and the Limits of Linear Thinking

insights.claim: A study cited from a prior podcast guest found that across a customer base, adopting AI coding tools resulted in roughly 300% more code being produced and roughly 400% more bugs, meaning defects grew faster than code volume.
insights.speaker: Shane Hastie
insights.so_what: A bug-growth rate that outpaces code-volume growth is a concrete data point that raw AI coding throughput gains can come with a disproportionate downstream quality-assurance cost.
insights.locator: More Code, More Bugs: AI as an Amplifier

insights.claim: A tech lead asked to review an AI-generated pull request spanning 27,000 lines changed across 104 files found it effectively impossible to review, illustrating that AI-generated code volume has broken the traditional line-by-line pull request review process even for experienced engineers.
insights.speaker: Joel Tosi
insights.so_what: A single AI-assisted PR this large shows code review capacity, not code generation capacity, is now the binding constraint in many AI-accelerated engineering workflows.
insights.quote: You don't. You can't. It's not possible, but I have to because I'm the tech lead.
insights.locator: More Code, More Bugs: AI as an Amplifier

themes.theme: Culture as Levers: Policy vs. Feeding

insights.claim: Culture is best defined as the unwritten rules and shared assumptions an organization safely relies on without discussing them, evidenced by hallmarks like shared language, shared humor, origin stories, and rituals, which is precisely what makes it hard to find deliberate levers to shape it.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Hendrickson
insights.so_what: Because culture is rarely discussed explicitly, leaders trying to change it need indirect, observational methods rather than direct edicts.
insights.locator: Defining Culture: The Unwritten Rules

insights.claim: Organizational levers split into two categories: policy, which only formal leadership can set (hiring criteria, job descriptions, org structure), and cultural 'feeding,' informal reinforcement that every person influences just by how they show up, whether intentionally or not.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Hendrickson
insights.so_what: This gives individual contributors, not just executives, a concrete category of actions (feeding) they can use to influence culture without needing formal authority.
insights.locator: Defining Culture: The Unwritten Rules

insights.claim: The core cultural-lever heuristic is to 'feed what you want to grow,' since culture cannot be dictated the way policy can; a simple example is expressing genuine appreciation for a specific behavior, like a small, easy-to-review pull request, which reinforces more of that behavior.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Hendrickson
insights.so_what: This reframes day-to-day praise and feedback as a deliberate, repeatable culture-shaping mechanism rather than a soft, optional nicety.
insights.locator: Feeding What You Want to Grow

insights.claim: A concrete feeding technique is reframing 'I'm stuck, who can help me?' into a proactive 'I'd like to work with someone today because I like to see what they see,' which feeds a culture of collaborative problem-solving instead of one where people default to working alone until something breaks.
insights.speaker: Joel Tosi
insights.so_what: Small, repeatable phrasing changes in team rituals are a low-cost, high-frequency way to visibly shift a team toward the collaborative culture leaders say they want.
insights.locator: Feeding What You Want to Grow

insights.claim: Reframing team demos from showing finished output to telling the story of what was surprising while building it feeds a curious, innovative culture rather than a pure status-reporting culture.
insights.speaker: Joel Tosi
insights.so_what: The format of a routine ritual like a demo is itself a culture lever, so redesigning recurring meetings is a practical, low-risk place to start feeding a desired culture.
insights.locator: Feeding What You Want to Grow

themes.theme: Seeing Before Acting: Work as Done vs. Work as Imagined

insights.claim: Meaningful change starts with seeing how work actually happens, because leaders typically operate on an outdated mental model of the job (work as imagined) based on old hands-on-keyboard experience, rather than the current visceral reality employees face, such as an engineer's job effectively becoming YAML configuration debugging.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Hendrickson
insights.so_what: Leaders should treat their own mental model of 'how the work gets done' as a hypothesis to test through direct observation, not as ground truth, especially post-AI-adoption when workflows change quickly.
insights.locator: Where to Start: Seeing Before Acting

insights.claim: Dashboards and status reports show curated, imagined signals of work, not the actual causal chain behind a problem; a volatile velocity metric might trace back through requirement misunderstanding to an architecture that was designed five years earlier for a different product, a chain only visible by being present with the team rather than reading a report.
insights.speaker: Joel Tosi
insights.so_what: Metrics dashboards alone systematically miss root causes; leaders who rely solely on them risk treating symptoms (volatility) instead of causes (outdated architecture).
insights.locator: Taylorism and the Separation of Strategy and Execution

insights.claim: Leaders can observe teams without becoming perceived micromanagers by first working to reduce fear in the culture, then using low-pressure entry points such as asking to sit in on a demo or asking what was surprising about building something, rather than directly auditing the work.
insights.speaker: Joel Tosi
insights.so_what: The sequencing matters: attempting direct observation in a low-safety culture will backfire by making people clam up, so culture work has to precede observational access.
insights.locator: Seeing Without Becoming a Micromanager

insights.claim: Receiving a signal about a problem does not obligate a leader to immediately pull a lever; deciding when and whether to act, and whether it is even that leader's lever to pull versus someone else's responsibility, is what distinguishes a well-informed manager from an over-reactive one.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Hendrickson
insights.so_what: This argues against reflexive intervention on every observed problem and for restraint, deferring to the person who actually owns the relevant lever.
insights.locator: Signals Don't Always Mean Pull the Lever

insights.claim: A leader can identify systemic problems without embedding in a specific team by pattern-matching recurring cross-team pain, such as outages that 'hop around' from one service to another to the DBA to DNS, which signals a deeper structural issue that more meetings, more policy, or a mandate for 'better monitoring' will not fix.
insights.speaker: Joel Tosi
insights.so_what: Recurring blame-shifting incident patterns are themselves diagnostic data; treating them as a symptom of a systemic gap rather than individual team failures points toward a structural fix instead of another policy layer.
insights.locator: Signals Don't Always Mean Pull the Lever

themes.theme: Psychological Safety and How Red Flags Get Heard

insights.claim: Whether raising a red flag results in being celebrated or being treated as the problem depends almost entirely on organizational context and culture, not on the objective severity of the issue being raised, since raising a genuinely serious risk can produce opposite receptions in different organizations.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Hendrickson
insights.so_what: Organizations should audit how their culture actually treats bad news in practice, since the same act of flagging risk can either surface or suppress critical information depending entirely on psychological safety.
insights.locator: Red Flags: The Skyscraper and the Tacoma Narrows Bridge

insights.claim: The historical Tacoma Narrows Bridge, nicknamed 'Galloping Gertie' for wobbling visibly in wind even during construction, is cited as a cautionary case where persistent public concern was dismissed by contemporary reporting as mere rider 'discomfort' rather than a structural risk, right up until the bridge collapsed from resonant-frequency failure.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Hendrickson
insights.so_what: A visible, repeated warning sign that is reframed as a minor annoyance rather than escalated as a structural risk is a pattern engineering organizations should actively watch for in their own incident histories.
insights.locator: Red Flags: The Skyscraper and the Tacoma Narrows Bridge

insights.claim: Asking for resources or support one lacks the authority to grant oneself, such as doubling cloud spend, increasing a token quota, or getting another team to partner more effectively, is itself a form of pulling a lever, since anyone always has the standing to articulate a need even without the authority to approve it.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Hendrickson
insights.so_what: This reframes escalation and asking for help as an active, legitimate management tool available to individual contributors, not a sign of weakness or failure to solve a problem independently.
insights.quote: Asking for help is pulling a lever.
insights.locator: Red Flags: The Skyscraper and the Tacoma Narrows Bridge

insights.claim: In a red/yellow/green status-reporting anecdote from a financial-data migration project, an accurate 'red' status (no data access, unknown formats, months before a January deadline) was progressively softened at each level of management to yellow and then green as each manager reframed the same facts more favorably for their own boss, and the project ultimately went live for one hour before being rolled back for two months.
insights.speaker: Joel Tosi
insights.so_what: Status distortion compounding up a management hierarchy is a directly observable, recurring organizational failure mode worth screening for in any project status-reporting process, especially ahead of hard deadlines.
insights.locator: The Watermelon Project: Red Inside, Green Outside

insights.claim: Building a thriving organization is not a single fix but constant care and course-correction, continuously watching for deviation from the desired culture and outcomes and making small nudges to bring the system back in line.
insights.speaker: Joel Tosi
insights.so_what: This argues against treating culture initiatives as one-time programs with a defined end date, favoring ongoing monitoring and small corrective actions instead.
insights.locator: Building a Thriving Organization

insights.claim: A leader rejected a team's proposal to fix low morale through team-building exercises, go-karts, and frequent hack days, arguing that if work isn't fun, the real sources of the problem, in this case unaddressed technical debt making daily work a slog, need to be fixed directly rather than papered over with surface-level fun activities.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Hendrickson
insights.so_what: This is a direct counter-argument to the common corporate playbook of adding perks to address low morale, arguing perks without root-cause fixes actively make things worse over time.
insights.locator: When "Fun" Papers Over Real Problems

insights.claim: Time spent on surface-level 'fun' activities is time not spent addressing the underlying sources of pain, which increases pain, which drives even more reliance on fun as a coping mechanism, a reinforcing loop that, left unaddressed, grinds an organization to a halt.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Hendrickson
insights.so_what: This names a specific vicious cycle (pain → fun band-aid → less time to fix pain → more pain) that leaders can watch for as a leading indicator their morale interventions are masking rather than solving a problem.
insights.locator: When "Fun" Papers Over Real Problems

insights.claim: The sequencing of work like technical-debt paydown is not fixed; optimizing for developer sense of purpose and job satisfaction produces a different priority order than optimizing for risk mitigation, so leaders must explicitly decide what they are optimizing for before choosing a sequence.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Hendrickson
insights.so_what: Two equally 'correct' technical-debt roadmaps can look completely different depending on the stated optimization goal, so leaders should make that goal explicit before sequencing work rather than assuming there's one obvious priority order.
insights.locator: When "Fun" Papers Over Real Problems

insights.claim: Every intervention should be treated as a testable bet: after optimizing for something, leaders need to verify whether the intended signal actually improved before continuing on that path, rather than assuming a change worked just because it was implemented.
insights.speaker: Joel Tosi
insights.so_what: This turns organizational change into an empirical, signal-driven loop rather than a one-time decision, meaning leaders should define success metrics for culture interventions upfront.
insights.locator: When "Fun" Papers Over Real Problems

themes.theme: Context Dependence: Right Today, Wrong Tomorrow

insights.claim: Because software delivery operates inside a constantly adapting system, an action that is correct today can become the wrong action tomorrow purely because the surrounding context has shifted, meaning there is no permanently correct policy for a given organizational problem.
insights.speaker: Joel Tosi
insights.so_what: Leaders should periodically re-validate standing policies against current context rather than treating past-correct decisions as permanently settled.
insights.locator: Favourite Parts of the Book

insights.claim: Using economic 'U-curve' models, a given context defines a range of good options, and as that context shifts the appropriate range shifts with it; for example, a team with zero automated testing should start with basic regression testing, but as that testing becomes more expensive at scale, investment should shift into other testing types.
insights.speaker: Joel Tosi
insights.so_what: This gives a concrete, modelable way to justify changing a testing (or other engineering-practice) strategy over time as a rational response to shifting cost curves, not as flip-flopping.
insights.locator: Favourite Parts of the Book

insights.claim: Early drafts of the book's fictional case-study company were deliberately made too mild, with small problems quickly overcome, and had to be rewritten with escalating, drawn-out hardship because realistic organizational change is messy and extended rather than resolved neatly within a short arc.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Hendrickson
insights.so_what: This is a meta-warning that simplified, quickly-resolved change narratives (in books, case studies, or consulting pitches) misrepresent how genuinely difficult and prolonged real organizational change actually is.
insights.locator: Favourite Parts of the Book
